title: When fine-tuning does not win
summary: A controlled comparison of LoRA, DoRA, and IA3 against zero-shot and few-shot math-reasoning baselines.
decision: Keep the model, data budget, and evaluation consistent, and publish negative results.

study.problem: Does parameter-efficient fine-tuning improve multi-step math reasoning when training data and compute are constrained?
study.built: Built a training and evaluation harness for LoRA, DoRA, and IA3, with answer extraction, per-category reporting, saved predictions, and zero-shot/five-shot baselines.
study.architecture: The adapter runs use Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, 6,000 examples, two epochs, seed 42, and a single V100 GPU. Evaluation records accuracy, extraction failures, latency, and output length. A ten-epoch IA3 follow-up probes longer training.

decisions.title: Keep the baseline visible
decisions.body: All three adapters underperformed the zero-shot model. IA3 is the best adapter in the recorded comparison, but not the best overall method.

decisions.title: Inspect more than accuracy
decisions.body: Track answer extraction failures and generation length alongside correctness to distinguish task failure from output-format behavior.

decisions.title: Test the longer-training hypothesis
decisions.body: IA3 accuracy fell from 0.6975 at two epochs to 0.6262 at ten. More epochs did not repair the gap under these conditions.

results.label: Zero-shot accuracy
results.context: Recorded GSM8K test evaluation, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, seed 42.

results.label: Best adapter: IA3
results.context: 6,000 training examples and two epochs; below the zero-shot baseline. LoRA: 63.99%; DoRA: 63.38%.

study.limitations: This is one model, dataset, seed, and constrained training recipe. The experiment does not establish a universal ranking of adapter methods. Identical hyperparameters are a controlled comparison, not per-method tuning.
study.lesson: A strong experiment can conclude that the simplest method is best for the tested budget.
